A future where his job disappears

NEW DELHI: When Major League Baseball (MLB) opened its office in India in 2019, it wasn't the beginning of its journey in India. It was the culmination of a 15-year wait.For Ryo Takahashi, MLB's Director of International Business and the man leading its operations in India, the timing wasn't driven by a grand strategic moment or a blockbuster announcement. It was simply when years of conversations finally turned into an official commitment."People think MLB suddenly discovered India in 2019," Takahashi said in a free-wheeling chat with TimesofIndia.com. "The reality is we had been discussing India for almost 15 years before opening the office. There wasn't a magical reason why it happened in 2019. That's simply when we received the approvals and could make the commitment official," he said.Seven years later, MLB's ambitions in India still look very different from those of most global sports leagues. There are no plans for a professional franchise, no immediate push for a domestic league and no obsession with television ratings. Instead, the league is betting on a deceptively simple idea: if enough children pick up a baseball, everything else will eventually follow.India became MLB's sixth international office after Japan, Mexico, China, the UK and the Dominican Republic.But unlike those markets, baseball arrived with almost no cultural footprint here. That forced the league to begin by listening rather than selling."We don't believe we have all the answers," Takahashi says. "The NBA, La Liga, the Premier League -- they've all spent years understanding Indian fans. I have friends and colleagues across those organisations, and we've learnt as much from their mistakes as their successes," he added.Rather than copying another league's blueprint, MLB chose to build its own Indian version: one centred on schools, grassroots coaching and local storytelling. Since 2019, it has introduced the First Pitch programme in schools across Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, launched the MLB Cup youth tournament and produced India-focused documentaries to make baseball feel more relatable.Ask Takahashi when India will produce its first Major League player, and he gently rejects the premise."People ask us when India will produce an MLB player. That's the wrong starting point," he says. "If one out of every hundred children who tries baseball decides to keep playing, that's already a victory. In a country of India's size, one per cent becomes a very big number."For MLB, participation is the primary currency, not finding elite talent."Our responsibility is to create opportunities. Whether that child eventually plays for an MLB club or simply falls in love with baseball, both outcomes help grow the sport," he reasoned.That thinking explains why MLB measures success through expanding coaching networks, more schools adopting baseball and the remarkable growth of the MLB Cup, which has evolved from just 12 teams in its inaugural edition into a nationwide youth competition involving thousands of participants.Conventional wisdom says cricket makes life impossible for another bat-and-ball sport. Takahashi argues the opposite."Cricket isn't our competitor. It might actually be our biggest advantage," he says. "Indian kids already grow up throwing, catching and hitting a ball. Those athletic foundations are already there," he explained.He has watched six-year-olds experience baseball for the first time and noticed how naturally many adapt."We don't have to teach them how to throw; we just have to show them a different game."MLB's objective isn't replacing cricket but borrowing from its ecosystem. Familiar movements reduce the learning curve, making baseball feel less foreign than many assume.Baseball's biggest obstacle in India isn't awareness alone. It's the clock.Most MLB games unfold in the early hours of the morning for Indian audiences, creating what Takahashi calls a classic chicken-and-egg problem.Even with broadcast partnerships in place with JioStar, he knows the league's target audience isn't awake."We want children to watch baseball, become curious and then play," he says. "But our games often happen at two or three in the morning in India.""An eight-year-old probably isn't holding the TV remote at that time. So maybe today's player becomes tomorrow's viewer. That's the journey we're trying to build."It's why MLB sees broadcasting as supporting grassroots rather than replacing it. A child introduced to baseball in school today may become the adult streaming the World Series a decade later.Perhaps Takahashi's most counterintuitive belief concerns infrastructure. While many emerging sports demand facilities first, MLB believes demand must precede concrete."People often say India needs baseball stadiums first," he says. "We actually think it works the other way around. First you create players, then you create demand, and eventually the infrastructure follows."He points to countless sporting cultures where children develop elite skills using improvised equipment and open spaces."Kids don't need a perfect baseball diamond to learn baseball. Skills come before stadiums."India already has cricket grounds, football fields and school playgrounds. For now, those are enough.That philosophy extends into MLB's biggest fan-facing initiative yet. Scheduled for October 24 in Mumbai, MLBX isn't designed as a traditional baseball tournament. It's a festival. Headed to the Mumbai Football Arena, Andheri Sports Complex, for MLBX are legends of the New York Yankees, Boston Red Sox, two-time defending champions Los Angeles Dodgers and Chicago Cubs."We asked ourselves: cricket evolved from Test matches to T20, football embraced futsal -- what’s baseball's version of that for India? MLBX is our answer," says Takahashi.The format features shorter games, compact fields, home-run contests, music performances and food inspired by classic American ballparks with Indian flavours. Baseball remains the centrepiece, but culture is the hook.The format or the tournament in itself is not new. MLBX is a mixed 3-on-3 baseball competition that combines power hitting, athletic defensive plays and fast-paced gameplay. The competition made its appearance during MLB All-Star Week in Philadelphia. The event has previously taken place at 15 US venues over the past three years, as well as internationally in London, Seoul and Mexico City."It's not just about games," Takahashi says. "It's home-run contests, music, food, culture and entertainment. We want someone to leave Mumbai thinking, 'That was fun... now let me find out more about baseball.'"He says the partnership with former India T20I captain and Mumbai Indians player Suryakumar Yadav has already generated a noticeable spike in enquiries, reinforcing MLB's belief that collaborating with cricket opens doors rather than closes them.Takahashi smiles when asked where he wants baseball in India to be by 2031. "My dream is to do such a good job that I make myself unemployed," he says almost with a grin.The answer is less about personal ambition than institutional success. He imagines an India with thousands more children playing baseball, a genuine national talent pathway, an active Indian national team and perhaps even baseball featuring if India hosts the 2036 Olympics."If, by 2031, baseball has become part of everyday sporting conversations in India, we've done our job," he says.For a league often associated with packed American ballparks and century-old rivalries, MLB's Indian strategy is strikingly patient. Its biggest victory may not be selling out a stadium. It may simply be convincing one child in a school playground to swap a cricket bat for a baseball bat.
Article Summary: Major League Baseball (MLB) opened its office in India in 2019. MLB's ambitions in India still look very different from those of most global sports leagues. There are no plans for a professional franchise, no immediate push for a domestic league. MLB is betting on a deceptively simple idea: if enough children pick up a baseball, everything else will eventually follow.

Article Title: Seven wickets in 21 balls: Sri Lanka's Chamari Athapaththu scripts history with record-breaking spell
Article Text:
Chamari Athapaththu

Defending champions Sri Lanka moved to the top of Group B in the Women's Asia Cup after beating Indonesia by 75 runs in Dubai on Thursday, thanks to captain Chamari Athapaththu's record seven-wicket haul and Nilakshika Silva's half-century.Sri Lanka were defending a modest target of 125 on a slow-paced pitch, but Athapaththu turned the match around with one of the best bowling performances in women's T20 internationals.She came on to bowl in the fourth over and struck with her fourth, seventh and eighth deliveries. Although she missed out on a hat-trick in that over, she completed it later by taking three wickets in three balls across two overs.Athapaththu finished with 7/5 in 21 balls, becoming the first bowler from a Full Member nation to take seven wickets in a women's T20I. The previous best figures in women's T20Is belonged to Zimbabwe's Esther Mbofana, who took 6/11 against Eswatini in 2021.Indonesia were bowled out for 49. Rahmawati Pangestuti scored 10, while Ni Made Putri Suwandewi remained unbeaten on 12. No other Indonesian batter reached double figures.Earlier, Sri Lanka were in trouble at 62/6 before Nilakshika Silva scored 50 off 35 balls to lift them to 124/7.For Indonesia, Ni Luh Dewi was the pick of the bowlers with 3/32.The win took Sri Lanka to the top of Group B in the Women's Asia Cup.In Group A, India remain on top of the standings, with Pakistan in second place.Meanwhile, India's vice-captain Smriti Mandhana also made history during India's Group A match against Hong Kong in Dubai. The 30-year-old went past Mithali Raj to become the highest run-scorer in women's international cricket across all formats.
Article Summary: Sri Lanka beat Indonesia by 75 runs in the Women's Asia Cup in Dubai. Captain Chamari Athapaththu took a record seven-wicket haul. Nilakshika Silva scored 50 off 35 balls to lift Sri Lanka to 124/7.

Article Title: ‘AAF risk’: Herbal supplements put India’s Asian Games athletes under scanner
Article Text:
Herbal Supplemets (Representational Image)

Unprecedented scrutiny

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bengaluru: With Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) officials conducting random checks on India’s elite athletes preparing for the Asian Games, experts are concerned that the use of herbal supplements by top athletes could result in Adverse Analytical Findings (AAF) when samples are tested for performance-enhancing substances at WADA-accredited laboratories abroad.According to experts, the use of herbal supplements is quite common among athletes training in national camps.“Among the supplements commonly used by our athletes are kida jadi buti, bhasmas, ashwagandha and shilajit. Kida jadi (Cordyceps sinensis) is the most expensive of the lot, retailing at Rs 16-20 lakh per kilogram. It is consumed after being mixed with honey,” they told TOI.In India, kida jadi is listed on e-commerce platforms at around Rs 1.66 lakh for 100g.“There are many athletes who use their savings to buy kida jadi and consume it regularly. There is a risk of an AAF for athletes using herbal supplements, as many of these products are not tested for their ingredients. For a month’s course, they may have to shell out around Rs 1 lakh.“A lot of our sprinters, throwers and middle-distance runners are taking these supplements,” they said, adding that most athletes do not disclose their use of herbal supplements when declaring the list of supplements they consume.Kida jadi is a type of fungus sourced from the Himalayas. Indian athletes have been using it for many years and none have returned a positive result so far. However, there have recently been concerns that some products may contain substances on WADA’s banned list, though nothing has been confirmed yet.“These metabolites may not have triggered a positive result in NADA tests, but in advanced tests conducted by the AIU, the outcome could be different, putting our athletes at risk of an AAF,” experts said.Asked about the use of locally sourced herbal supplements, Mihira Khopkar, who served as the Indian contingent’s nutritionist at the Paris Olympics, confirmed the risks involved.“In elite sport, it is almost non-negotiable that high-performing athletes choose supplements that are not only evidence-based but also third-party tested,” she told TOI.Athletics coaches, both former and current, who have followed India’s progress over the past few decades, recalled that Indian athletes have never undergone such intense testing before a major Games.“What the AIU has done on behalf of WADA is targeted testing of India’s top athletes who will be competing at the Asian Games. Across Bengaluru, Bhubaneswar and Patiala, officials have tested most athletes in the squad. This is the first time they have conducted such large-scale random testing of Indian athletes ahead of a major meet,” sources told TOI.“A few years ago, WADA attempted to test Indian athletes training in Potchefstroom, South Africa, but achieved limited success as many were unavailable. Athletes cannot be penalised for missing random tests, unlike those in the Registered Testing Pool (RTP), who are bound by the whereabouts clause,” they added.After testing athletes residing at the Kalinga Stadium complex in Bhubaneswar, officials also conducted checks on those training in Bengaluru at the Anju Bobby Sports Foundation and the SAI South Centre.India topped the AIU’s list of doping offenders in July this year with 162 names, ahead of Kenya (148) and Russia (60). The AIU also reclassified the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) from Category B to Category A.“Unfortunately, the quality of the domestic anti-doping programme is simply not proportionate to the doping risk,” AIU Chair David Howman had said.
Article Summary: The Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) is conducting random checks on India’s elite athletes preparing for the Asian Games. Experts are concerned that the use of herbal supplements could result in Adverse Analytical Findings (AAF) when samples are tested for performance-enhancing substances abroad.

Article Title: 'A bit abnormal': After shock second-round exit at US Open, Auger-Aliassime reveals he 'was seeing spots'
Article Text:
Felix Auger-Aliassime, of Canada, serves the ball to Karen Khachanov, of Russia, during the second round of the U.S. Open tennis championships Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Karen Khachanov knocked out third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime from the US Open on Thursday, winning 6-7(5), 6-3, 6-2, 6-2 to reach the third round.The Russian, ranked No. 50 in the world, came into the tournament after losing the opening match in all three of his US Open warm-up events. But he took advantage of an off-colour Auger-Aliassime, whose level dropped as the match went on at Louis Armstrong Stadium.After the match, Auger-Aliassime said he started feeling unwell during the contest and struggled to recover."After a set and a half, I just couldn't feel well and was dizzy and seeing spots and couldn't recover," he said, as quoted by BBC. "I thought maybe it would pass, but it didn't."I've never felt quite like that. I've had cramps before. I've felt tired towards the end of matches, but in a normal way."This was abnormal a little bit, and there were no signs in the last couple of days and no signs this morning, as well."The defeat made Auger-Aliassime the highest-ranked player to exit the men's singles draw so far in New York.Khachanov, who reached the US Open semi-finals in 2022, broke the Canadian's serve seven times during the match. He also saved seven of the nine break points he faced.The win is only Khachanov's second victory over a top-10 player at a Grand Slam and sends him into the third round in New York.The result meant Khachanov has now reached the third round of all four Grand Slam tournaments in a single ​calendar year for the first time.
Article Summary: Karen Khachanov knocked out third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime from the US Open. Russian, ranked No. 50 in the world, won 6-7(5), 6-3, 6-2,6-2 to reach the third round.

Former world No. 1 Kidambi Srikanth produced a stunning comeback to upset world No. 9 Victor Lai of Canada, while the men’s doubles pair of Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty battled a mid-match slump to reach the quarterfinals of the China Masters Super 750 badminton tournament in Shenzhen on Thursday.There was disappointment, however, for young Tanvi Sharma and the mixed doubles pair of Dhruv Kapila and Tanisha Crasto.Tanvi fought hard against Japan’s Tomoka Miyazaki but went down 17-21, 21-18, 16-21.Dhruv and Tanisha suffered an 18-21, 18-21 defeat to Liu Kuang Heng and Hsu Yin Hui of Chinese Taipei.Srikanth, the 2021 World Championships silver medallist, displayed remarkable fighting spirit to overcome World Championships bronze medallist Lai 21-18, 21-19.Later, he said: “I was only thinking about what I have been doing throughout the match and what I need to do going forward.”Srikanth added: “He has been playing well for the last 12-14 months. But I felt I’ll have my chances if I can play my best. I wasn’t thinking about how he has been playing. I was only thinking about how I should play.”Srikanth will next take on Hong Kong’s Lee Cheuk Yiu for a place in the semifinals.Meanwhile, Satwiksairaj and Chirag overcame a determined challenge from Frenchmen Christo Popov and Toma Junior Popov to register a 21-15, 22-24, 21-9 victory.They now face the Danish pair of Kim Astrup and Anders Skaarup Rasmussen in the quarterfinals.

Article Title: Treesa-Gayatri’s coach missing from list, WFI finally clears foreign coaches
Article Text:
India's Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand Pullela (ANI Photo)

New Delhi:

WFI finally relents on foreign coaches

Only seven grooms in equestrian

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In squash, Willstrop will be foreign coach

Hockey without women’s masseuse

India’s latest women’s doubles hope, BWF World Championships bronze medallists Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand, will head to the Asian Games without their dedicated coach B Sumeeth Reddy, whose name does not figure in the official coaching and support staff list for badminton, while the Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) has finally agreed to send all three foreign coaches despite its initial reluctance, following a Sports Authority of India (SAI) rebuke.Reddy, a former Olympian who retired in March 2025, has specifically worked with Treesa and Gayatri since then, while also overseeing other women’s doubles players at the Pullela Gopichand Academy in Hyderabad. He was a constant presence in their coaching corner at international events and during the recent Worlds in New Delhi, sitting alongside Gopichand and guiding the pair through their matches.Treesa and Gayatri ended India’s 15-year wait for a women’s doubles medal at the Worlds since 2011, producing a string of impressive performances to claim bronze.Their Asian Games place had earlier come under scrutiny after sports authorities questioned their selection against the prescribed criteria, with Priya Konjengbam and Shruti Mishra emerging as alternatives. Badminton Association of India (BAI) defended the selection on rankings and recent performances.TOI contacted a senior federation official to ascertain whether Reddy’s name had originally been forwarded to the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) as an official women’s doubles coach.A call to a BAI official did not elicit a response.It has been learnt that Gopichand will carry the primary responsibility of guiding Treesa and Gayatri in Reddy’s absence. Tan Kim Her, who specifically works with Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, could assist the women’s pair if schedules do not clash. South Korean Yong Sung Yoo, Lakshya Sen’s personal coach has received clearance. Twelve coaching and support personnel have been named for the 20-member badminton team.For wrestling’s 16-member squad, 14 coaching and support personnel have been listed, with all three foreign coaches now set to travel: Georgia’s Emzarios Bentinidis (men’s freestyle), Russia’s Gogi Koguashvili (greco-roman) and Japan’s Kosei Akaishi (women’s team). WFI had initially resisted sending them, preferring Indian coaches over them, but agreed after SAI questioned their omission.According to sources, the Equestrian Federation of India’s (EFI) ad-hoc committee had proposed 20 grooms for the eight-member equestrian team, but only seven have received clearance. The 12-member coaching and support staff list includes Nico Wienstroer, Katharina Asbeck, Kyra Anne Jonkers, Jill Van Osselt, Tabea Linhardt, Johanna Aini Katariina Pohjonen and Alyson Renee Roy as the seven grooms.SAI had also sought an explanation over the original proposal, with no groom named for dressage rider Jai Sud or eventing specialist Arjan Nagra.Former world No. 1 James Willstrop has been granted the SAI’s clearance to serve as India’s foreign squash coach receiving the nod for the same. The Englishman is expected to arrive in Chennai on Sept 17 before travelling with the team.The 40-member hockey squad has 14 support staff, and male masseur Arup Naskar is the sole masseur listed.
Article Summary: Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand will head to the Asian Games without their dedicated coach B Sumeeth Reddy. The Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) has finally agreed to send all three foreign coaches despite its initial reluctance. Former world No. 1 James Willstrop has been granted the SAI's clearance to serve as India’s foreign squash coach receiving the nod for the same.

Article Title: Neeraj Chopra’s replacement: Yashvir Singh drafted into India’s Asian Games javelin squad
Article Text:
India's Neeraj Chopra, right, and Yashvir Singh in a photograph after the men's javelin throw final at the Commonwealth Games 2026. (PTI Photo)

New Delhi:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Know Yashvir

Glasgow Commonwealth Games bronze medallist javelin thrower Yashvir Singh has been drafted into India’s Asian Games athletics squad, replacing two-time Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra , who was ruled out for the season following an ankle ligament tear.Yashvir, who recently threw a personal best of 85.41m at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, will team up with the in-form Rohit Yadav (personal best 87.05m) to anchor India’s two-member men’s javelin campaign at Aichi-Nagoya.Meanwhile, former long jumper and Athletics Federation of India (AFI) senior vice-president Anju Bobby George will not travel as team leader, it’s been learnt. Though proposed by the AFI, her name was not cleared by the sports ministry adhering to its guidelines which say: IOA will ensure that any person, if he/she is holding elected position in EC of IOA, any NSF or any sports body, whose name has been included in the list of team officials, will be treated at no cost to the govt.The final athletics squad strength has been pruned to 77. Distance runner Abhishek Pal was dropped after testing positive for clomiphene. “It is not a case of returning dope positive, but as National Anti Doping Agency (NADA) investigates, we don’t want to take any risks,” said AFI planning committee chairman Lalit Bhanot. Additionally, 110m hurdler Tejas Shirse was ruled out due to foot stress fractures suffered during CWG.These two exclusions offset the latest addition of six athletes — Harita Bhadra (200m), Kiran Pahal (400m), Sindhushree G (pole vault), I Asha Ilango (triple jump), Sanya Yadav (discus), and Praveen Kumar (hammer throw) — who were cleared by the ministry after the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) accepted IOA’s late request for their addition, bringing the count from 73 to 79 before Pal and Shirse’s omissions brought the contingent size down to 77.AFI is also seeking approval for Hangzhou double-medallist Avinash Sable to compete in the 5,000m alongside his confirmed 3,000m steeplechase event. However, Sable must first breach the AFI qualification mark of 13:39.18s at the Indian Athletics Series Finals here on Sept 10, where most Asian Games-bound athletes will compete.-- Born in Devsar, Haryana and raised in Jaipur, Raj.-- Shifted from basketball to javelin at age 13, initially practicing with bamboo javelins.-- Coached by his father Rai Singh, a former Indian Railways national champion.-- Broke Chopra’s U-20 Federation Cup record in 2021; joined the 80m club in 2022 (82.13m).-- Overcame major shoulder surgery in late 2023 that kept him out for nearly a year.-- Claimed bronze at Glasgow CWG with a final-throw personal best of 85.41m.-- Became only the third Indian male javelin medallist in CWG history after Kashinath Naik and Chopra.
Article Summary: Yashvir Singh replaces two-time Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra. Chopra ruled out for the season following an ankle ligament tear. Former long jumper Anju Bobby George will not travel as team leader. Distance runner Abhishek Pal dropped after testing positive for clomiphene.

Article Title: 'Encroacher' remark hangs over Yusuf Pathan as former India cricketer turned politician withdraws Gujarat high court appeal over Vadodara land dispute: Case explained
Article Text:
Yusuf Pathan (ANI Photo)

Pathan had challenged land allotment rejection

MP Yusuf Pathan during the Monsoon session of Parliament, in New Delhi. (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

VMC had asked Pathan to vacate plot

Yusuf Pathan campaigns with Rana Chatterjee (PTI Photo)

The Gujarat High Court on Monday dismissed as withdrawn an appeal filed by former India cricketer and Lok Sabha MP Yusuf Pathan against a single-judge order that had described him as an “encroacher” on a piece of government land in Vadodara.Pathan’s lawyer, Shalin Mehta, sought permission to withdraw the plea before a division bench comprising Chief Justice Sunita Agarwal and Justice DN Ray. The lawyer told the court that Pathan’s claim over the land was still being pursued under a state government policy.The division bench subsequently dismissed the appeal as withdrawn.The 43-year-old had approached the High Court challenging a single-judge order that upheld the Gujarat government’s decision to reject his request for allotment of the 978-square metre plot owned by the Vadodara Municipal Corporation (VMC).Pathan had claimed the land under a state policy applicable to international cricketers.During an earlier hearing, Pathan had told the court that he was pursuing his claim under a state government scheme and was given four weeks to pursue the matter. The High Court had also warned that he could face higher payment of damages if he took longer to vacate the plot.During Monday’s proceedings, Mehta said they were awaiting a response from the VMC but had not received one.“Because we are saying that there is a circular which allows international cricketers to be given a plot. I think I will withdraw because I haven’t heard anything from them (VMC). I have taken instructions from my client…if it is to happen, it will happen outside the court; otherwise it won’t happen," Mehta submitted.With the appeal withdrawn, Pathan’s attempt to challenge the earlier court order through the division bench has come to an end.The dispute dates back to 2024, when the Gujarat government rejected Pathan’s request for allotment of the plot. Despite the rejection, he continued to occupy the land.After Pathan was elected from the Baharampur Lok Sabha seat in West Bengal on a Trinamool Congress (TMC) ticket in 2024, the VMC issued him a notice asking him to vacate the land. Pathan refused and challenged the matter in court.The High Court had previously taken a strong view of his occupation of the plot. During a hearing on June 8, the court came down heavily on Pathan over the alleged “encroachment” and orally questioned how he could enter and occupy the land without completing the required formalities.The matter now moves outside the court as Pathan continues to pursue his claim under the state policy.
Article Summary: Gujarat High Court dismisses appeal filed by former India cricketer Yusuf Pathan. Pathan had challenged a single-judge order that had described him as an “encroacher’ on a piece of government land in Vadodara. The 43-year-old had approached the High Court challenging the decision.

Article Title: 'Too many matches': BCCI admits packed schedule is a challenge, plans better FTP
Article Text:
India Test and ODI captain Shubman Gill

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The BCCI will look to ensure Indian cricketers get enough rest, time to acclimatise and practice matches before major series in SENA countries, secretary Devajit Saikia said on Thursday.Saikia was speaking after a review meeting at the BCCI headquarters, which discussed India's recent performances and the team's plans for the next year.He said there was no communication gap within Indian cricket on injury management, but acknowledged that the Future Tours Programme (FTP) could be planned better to give players more time to prepare.“Everybody is on the same page. BCCI is working in a very well like a well oiled engine," Saikia told reporters."There is proper coordination amongst all the wings of BCCI, whether it is women's teams committees or their technical staff or their coaches, vis-a-vis the COE, vis-a-vis the Indian men's team’s coaching staff and the head coach. There is no difficulty in the coordination, everything is moving in the right direction.”Saikia said the number of matches being played in a year remains the main challenge for the board.“The only challenge which we are facing is that there are too many matches in the year and that is why in the next FTP we will do certain things, we will take certain measures.“We have instructed our FTP persons who will be meeting very soon in various international forums that our FTP should be in such a way it should be scheduled that there is proper rest for the players as well as some kind of acclimatisation or some kind of friendly matches before any major series in SENA countries (South Africa, Australia, England and New Zealand),” Saikia added.The meeting was attended by India Test and ODI captain Shubman Gill, T20I captain Shreyas Iyer, head coach Gautam Gambhir , director of cricket at the Centre of Excellence VVS Laxman and other BCCI officials. Selection committee chairman Ajit Agarkar could not join the meeting, even through video conferencing.Saikia said the meeting covered India's performances in England and Ireland and the team's plans for the next year.“We discussed (about) our team performed in England and Ireland and also about what we are going to do about the next one year. The road map has been prepared and we will be doing some exercises so that we have a very good performance in 2027 (ODI) World Cup,” Saikia added.He also acknowledged that India had not done well on their limited-overs tours of Ireland and England. Saikia said the team needed to do some “soul searching”, while adding that a strategy had been “chalked out” in that regard.India lost the two-match T20I series against Ireland 0-2 before losing the T20I series against England 1-4 and the three-match ODI series 1-2.
Article Summary: The BCCI will look to ensure Indian cricketers get enough rest, time to acclimatise and practice matches before major series in SENA countries, secretary Devajit Saikia said on Thursday.Saikia was speaking after a review meeting at the BCCI headquarters, which discussed India's recent performances and the team's plans for the next year.

Article Title: 65m boundaries, hybrid pitch: Inside the new venue for India’s Asian Games campaign
Article Text:
Indian cricket team (PTI)

Drainage a key issue

Chennai: India’s gold medal defence in cricket at the Asian Games will begin in the quarterfinals on September 28, and there could well be a blockbuster game against Pakistan a couple of days later.The site of three baseball grounds has been converted into a new facility in Nisshin called Korogi Sports Park, where Japan will get a taste of top-flight cricket.For starters, it’s not as small a ground as the one used during the Hangzhou Asiad four years ago. The shortest boundary at Nisshin is 65 metres, almost 10 metres longer than the facility that hosted cricket at Hangzhou.Adam Birss, technical operations manager for cricket at the Asiad, told TOI that this was possible because the organisers were able to build a ground from scratch, giving them the liberty to use more space, which wasn’t the case in Hangzhou.To help with the preparation of the pitches, the Asian Cricket Council reached out to Sri Lanka Cricket, which sent Asitha Wijayasinghe, the curator of Kandy’s Pallekele International Stadium.Given Pallekele’s high-scoring nature, it will be safe to assume that the facility in Nisshin will see a lot of runs being scored. It can be a welcome relief from what we saw when part of the T20 World Cup in 2024 was held at a makeshift venue at Nassau County ground near New York, with teams struggling to manage 125.In addition to four turf pitches, the ground also has a hybrid pitch consisting of natural clay and synthetic fibres, the technology being used in Australia and Sri Lanka.“The construction allows us to prepare a faster pitch. It is also more forgiving in terms of wear and tear,” Birss said.The clay used for the pitches is local. “The clay content will not only provide bounce for pacers, but also grip for spinners,” Birss added.One of the biggest concerns will be the risk of typhoons, which typically strike Japan around the window in which the Games are scheduled to be held. This makes drainage an important aspect, and Birss informed that adequate measures are being taken.“The ground has been reinforced with a sand base, allowing for more water absorption. However, given that the ground was built with a tight public budget, the drainage cannot be compared with the best around the world,” Birss said.
Article Summary: The site of three baseball grounds has been converted into a new facility in Nisshin called Korogi Sports Park. India’s gold medal defence in cricket at the Asian Games will begin in the quarterfinals on September 28, and there could well be a blockbuster game against Pakistan a couple of days later.

NEW DELHI: Smriti Mandhana has already established herself among the finest batters in women's cricket, but on Thursday she reached a new pinnacle — becoming the most prolific run-scorer in the history of the women's game.During India's Women's Asia Cup 2026 clash against Hong Kong China in Dubai, the Indian vice-captain surpassed legendary former captain Mithali Raj 's tally of 10,868 international runs to become the highest run-scorer in women's international cricket across all formats.And she did it in spectacular fashion.Mandhana produced a breathtaking 124 off 64 balls, smashing 14 fours and seven sixes at a strike rate of 193.75 as India posted 193/5 after being asked to bat first. Her record-breaking innings not only took her past Mithali but also established a series of new milestones.Mandhana entered the match knowing she was closing in on Mithali's long-standing record. Having already overtaken New Zealand great Suzie Bates to move into second place during the Asia Cup opener against Thailand, the 30-year-old needed one more major push to rewrite the all-time record.She delivered far more than that.Mandhana initially had to negotiate a slow Dubai surface and disciplined Hong Kong bowling. Shafali Verma provided the early acceleration, with the opening pair putting on 50 before Verma departed for 28 off 17 balls.Once Mandhana settled in, however, the innings changed gears.She reached her half-century and then launched an extraordinary assault, moving from 50 to 100 in just 17 deliveries. Her century came off 57 balls before she eventually finished with 124 from 64, her second T20I hundred.Her dismissal came on the final over of the innings following a mix-up with Bharti Fulmali, but by then Mandhana had already rewritten the record books.The 124 also became the highest individual score in Women's T20 Asia Cup history, surpassing Chamari Athapaththu's unbeaten 119 against Malaysia in 2024.Mandhana's landmark innings did not stop with the all-time runs record.Her century took her international hundred tally to 18, making her the leading century-maker in women's international cricket, ahead of Australia's Meg Lanning and South Africa's Laura Wolvaardt, who had 17 each.She also became the first Indian woman to score two T20I centuries. Her previous hundred had come against England in 2025, when she made 112.The latest innings also extended Mandhana and Shafali's remarkable partnership record. Their 50-plus stand against Hong Kong was their 29th in T20Is, the most by any pair in the format.For Mandhana, though, the most significant achievement was undoubtedly moving past Mithali.Mithali's 10,868 runs had stood as the benchmark of women's international batting excellence since her retirement in 2022. Mandhana's explosive rise has now taken her beyond that mark, with New Zealand's Suzie Bates, England's Charlotte Edwards and West Indies great Stafanie Taylor completing the top five on the all-time list.What made Thursday's achievement even more remarkable was the manner in which Mandhana reached it. On a surface that offered little pace, she adapted her game, used the back foot effectively and found ways to manufacture boundaries.“Having said that, I just love batting, and I’m happy that I could contribute,” Mandhana said during the mid-innings break.
Article Summary: Smriti Mandhana becomes the most prolific run-scorer in women's cricket. Indian vice-captain surpasses former captain Mithali Raj's tally of 10,868 international runs. She produced a breathtaking 124 off 64 balls, smashing 14 fours and seven sixes at a strike rate of 193.75.

NEW DELHI: The Board of Control for Cricket in India ( BCCI ) is taking a long-term view of Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's astonishing rise, with secretary Devajit Saikia revealing that the board is closely monitoring the 15-year-old and wants to ensure his early success translates into a long and distinguished international career.Sooryavanshi's rapid emergence was among the matters discussed at Thursday's high-level BCCI review meeting in Mumbai, which was attended by Saikia, India Test and ODI captain Shubman Gill , T20I captain Shreyas Iyer, head coach Gautam Gambhir, Centre of Excellence (CoE) head VVS Laxman and other senior officials.The teenager has already gone from being an IPL sensation to becoming India's youngest men's international debutant, and the BCCI is now determined to ensure that his development is handled carefully rather than allowing the weight of expectation to derail his progress.“We want Vaibhav Sooryavanshi or any player of his stature to continue and serve like Sachin Tendulkar did for the country or other players who in the past became legends,” Saikia said.“So we look at Vaibhav in a very serious manner. He's monitored from every angle and every step he is taking forward in his international career. The BCCI is taking a very close look at his future.”Saikia made it clear that the BCCI's objective is not simply to maximise Sooryavanshi's immediate impact but to build a career that can last for years.“You see, the BCCI can be proud that we are promoting a player of the age of 15 years who is already making his mark in the international scenario and we are very cautious that every right step he should take forward so that it should not be a one series or one year wonder,” he said.The comparison with Tendulkar was particularly significant. Like Sooryavanshi, Tendulkar was thrust into the international spotlight as a teenager before going on to enjoy one of the longest and most successful careers in the history of the game.The BCCI secretary stressed that Sooryavanshi's progress would be closely tracked at every stage.“We want Vaibhav's relevance, or any player of his stature, to continue and serve as Sachin Tendulkar did for the country or other players who in the past became legends,” Saikia said.The teenager's rapid rise has given the board plenty of reason for optimism. He was India's youngest-ever men's international debutant after earning his maiden call-up following a sensational IPL 2026 campaign with Rajasthan Royals.Sooryavanshi scored 776 runs in 16 matches at a strike rate of 237.30, including a century and five fifties, while his 72 sixes set an IPL record for a single season. He subsequently won several awards, including the Orange Cap, Most Valuable Player, Emerging Player, Super Striker and Super Sixes honours.He also made an immediate impact for India against Zimbabwe, scoring 151 runs in three matches as India completed a 3-0 sweep and claimed his maiden Player of the Series award.His development has continued in domestic cricket. At 15 years and 157 days, he recently became the youngest batter to score a half-century in Duleep Trophy history, breaking a record that had stood for 57 years.Importantly, the BCCI's focus is not limited to Sooryavanshi. Saikia revealed that the board has identified a larger group of emerging players who are being monitored through the CoE.“That our selectors are looking, we have a huge number of upcoming players who are doing good. If you look at our U19 Indian team, they are becoming champions recently also. Similarly, in women's cricket also, we are world champions for the last two international U19 T20 World Cups,” he said.“So we are looking at all the players, not only Vaibhav's relevance, but there are about 10-15 players who are in our targeted group. Those are named in our targeted group list, and they are constantly monitored by our COE head, VVS Laxman, who is taking keen interest in their future and their training and skill development.”Laxman's direct involvement gives Sooryavanshi and the other youngsters access to the BCCI's central development structure as they make the difficult transition from age-group cricket to senior international cricket.The approach also reflects the board's desire to avoid rushing talented youngsters simply because of their early success.
Article Summary: The Board of Control for Cricket in India is taking a long-term view of Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's astonishing rise. NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Share your view.

Article Title: ‘That video was not ordinary’: PM Modi praises Lovlina for objecting to distorted India map - Watch
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi shares a light moment with boxer Lovlina Borgohain. (PTI Photo)

‘That video was not ordinary’

Mirabai opens up about four difficult years

Narender's joke leaves Modi laughing

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.
Article Summary: Lovlina Borgohain won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time. India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.

Article Title: ‘From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping’: PM Modi’s heartfelt message to CWG heroes - Watch
Article Text:
PM Narendra Modi interacted with India's CWG 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday. (Pic credit: PM Modi's X post)

Mirabai recalls four years of struggle

‘One family will bring three medals’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India’s Glasgow success

NEW DELHI: “From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping.”Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an emotional message for Mirabai Chanu as he interacted with India's Commonwealth Games 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday, reflecting on the sacrifices behind the country's successful campaign in Glasgow.Modi hosted the medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg and heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys at the Games. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze, finishing fourth in the overall standings.During one of the conversations, Modi recalled the emotional scenes surrounding Mirabai's gold-medal triumph.“Tears were falling from you. I feel as if from every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping,” Modi told the Olympic silver medallist.Mirabai, who won gold in Glasgow, opened up about the difficult journey that preceded her Commonwealth Games triumph, including the disappointment of the Paris Olympics.“I was very happy, and emotional too. That day the happiness was greater and I cried because at the Paris Olympics, I lost a medal by 1 kg. In a player’s life what all we have to face. So within these 4 years, how much and what all I had faced, every time injuries were going on and all that was happening.So with great difficulty I had faced these 4 years. So when all that happened, on the podium when I stood, sir, and when our flag goes up and our national anthem plays, sir, we cannot stop, sir, tears come out on their own,” she said.Modi responded by highlighting the wider impact of the athletes' achievements.“This is very good. It is not as if this achievement of yours is considered only your achievement; your victory becomes a very big inspiration for the coming generations.”The informal interaction also saw athletes share lighter and deeply personal moments from their Glasgow campaigns.Modi reminded para shot put gold medallist Sharmila Dhankar of a promise she had made earlier.“You made a promise. Last time, yours, both daughters will become players,” Modi said with a smile.Dhankar replied: “Haanji, right now they are young in age. In the next Commonwealth, one family will bring 3 medals.”Men's 100m T47 gold medallist Dilip Gavit, meanwhile, spoke about dedicating his performance to his guru.“When I was running, when my event was on 29th (July), that day was Guru Purnima, so that day I gave a gift to my guru,” he was heard saying in the video.In another video posted by Modi, gold medallist boxer Sakshi Chaudhary introduced herself and the contingent.“Hello friends! This is Sakshi Chaudhary. Today, our honourable Prime Minister has invited us, the Commonwealth Games medalists, and we feel very proud. We are extremely happy to have met him; he is very humble. Sir, would you like to say something?” she said.Modi replied with a message that summed up his interaction with the athletes: “Jo khelega, woh khilega” (The one who plays, will blossom). “Always cheer for Bharat.”India's fourth-place finish came despite a significantly smaller contingent and a reduced sporting programme compared to Birmingham 2022. India sent 122 athletes to Glasgow, compared to 210 in Birmingham, while 30 of its 61 medals in 2022 came in sports that were not part of the Glasgow programme.Despite those limitations, India retained its fourth-place position and improved its medal conversion rate, with 38 athletes returning home with medals. Long-distance runner Gulveer Singh was the only Indian athlete to win two medals.The Glasgow Games concluded after 11 days, with Scotland handing over the Commonwealth Games flag and ceremonial baton to India ahead of the 2030 edition in Ahmedabad.The symbols were handed to Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha and Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi during the closing ceremony.Ahmedabad will become only the second Indian city to host the Commonwealth Games after New Delhi staged the 2010 edition.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi hosted medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg. Modi heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze.

Article Title: From hospital bed to CWG gold: How Jaismine Lamboria fought the odds in Glasgow
Article Text:
India's Jaismine Lamboria celebrates after winning the women's 57kg boxing final. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Just weeks before stepping into the ring at the Commonwealth Games, Jaismine Lamboria wasn’t thinking about medals. She was searching for answers. The recurring fever had refused to go away.Multiple medical tests showed nothing unusual and the Indian boxer tried to push through, managing the symptoms with paracetamol. When the illness persisted, she was admitted to a hospital in Mohali. Doctors finally diagnosed a bacterial infection, putting her on an intensive 14-day course of medication. For an athlete preparing for one of the biggest competitions of the year, it could easily have been the end of the campaign.Instead, it became the beginning of one of the most remarkable comebacks of her career. “I was avoiding further medical tests because the initial reports were coming back normal. We didn’t know what exactly had to be treated. Finally, after I was admitted, they detected a bacterial infection and I was on medication for 14 days,” the 57kg boxer said.When she was discharged, the clock was already ticking. Barely three weeks remained before the Games.“I started training only on July 1. Initially it was just warm-up, walking and stretching. I had very little time, so we had to be patient.”The physical recovery was only one part of the challenge. During those uncertain weeks, sports psychologist Priya Vrinda became a constant source of support, ensuring the illness didn’t break her confidence.“When I was sick, I was already connected with Priya Vrinda ma’am. She kept me mentally strong and never allowed me to go down,” Jaismine said. That resilience was evident when she returned to competition. Jaismine boxed with maturity, tactical discipline and composure to upgrade the Commonwealth bronze she had won four years ago into gold in the 57kg.One of Jaismine’s biggest assets inside the ring has been her reach in her category. While every opponent may not be shorter — Jaismine stands five feet seven inches in her socks — she believes her physical advantage has become an important weapon thanks to careful coaching. “My coaches taught me how to use my reach properly. It definitely gives me an advantage in many bouts.”
Article Summary: Jaismine Lamboria won gold in the women's 57kg boxing at the Commonwealth Games. The Indian boxer had been suffering from a recurring fever. Doctors diagnosed a bacterial infection and put her on a 14-day course of medication. Jaismine credits her coach Priya Vrinda with helping her recover.

Article Title: How Jadumani Singh's risky weight change nearly derailed his CWG dream before winning Glasgow silver
Article Text:
India's Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (PTI Photo)

A bold gamble after the 50kg category disappeared

The selection maze before Glasgow

Jadumani Si​ngh's Road to CWG Silver (AI-generated Infographic)

The Sports Ministry hurdle

Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (PTI Photo)

Why the gold slipped away

File Pic: L Sarita Devi (PTI Photo)

Olympic gold remains the ultimate dream

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: When Indian pugilist Jadumani Singh Mandengbam stepped onto the podium to receive the men's 55kg silver medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, it marked the culmination of a journey that had almost ended before it had even begun.The 22-year-old Manipuri boxer was one of India's standout performers, winning four consecutive unanimous 5-0 verdicts to storm into the bantamweight final before settling for silver against Australia's Jye Dixon. His medal also formed part of India's historic boxing campaign, which yielded seven golds and three silvers, making the country the No. 1 boxing nation at the Games for the first time.Yet, behind that success lay months of uncertainty, selection hurdles and a weight-category gamble that nearly cost him a place on the flight to Scotland.Speaking exclusively to TimesofIndia.com, former world champion and Jadumani's mentor, Laishram Sarita Devi, recounted how the young boxer refused to abandon his Olympic dream even when every obstacle seemed stacked against him.Jadumani had built his reputation in the 50kg category, winning medals at World Boxing Cups before learning that the division would no longer feature in the Commonwealth Games, Asian Games or Olympic programme.Rather than remain in a non-Olympic category, he decided to move up to 55kg — a division already occupied by some of India's biggest names."He continued to consult with me. Whenever he had to make a big decision, he called up and consulted with me — like increasing his weight category," Sarita told TimesofIndia.com."After he won a World Cup medal in 50kg, he got to know that the weight category is no longer in the CWG, Asian Games and Olympics. He wanted to move to 55kg."The decision immediately brought fresh challenges."Army had their No. 1 boxer in the 55kg category in Pune, who is Services' No. 1 boxer. And the weight category also has Amit Panghal — Olympian and Asian champion. He said he wanted to move up the weight to compete at CWG, Asian Games etc, but was discouraged by hearing questions like whether he would be able to compete at that level, which created a doubt in him," she said.Sarita, however, wanted only one answer: "We sat down and I asked him, 'Are you confident about the decision?' He said he was, so I told him to move up the category."The decision created another problem.Without competing in the National Championships, Jadumani could not enter the national coaching camp. But because he belonged to the Army Sports Institute, Services already had its designated 55kg representative. Attempts to let him represent Manipur also failed."We tried to make him compete for the state of Manipur, but we didn't get an NOC because he is with the Army," Sarita said.Relief finally arrived through a Boxing Federation of India (BFI) policy that granted direct entries to the National Championships for World Boxing Cup medallists. The move was aimed at rewarding elite international performers and ensuring they were not blocked by the usual domestic qualification pathways.The decision allowed Jadumani to compete directly in the 55kg draw despite the institutional overlap, resulting in multiple squad members — Pawan Bartwal, Jadumani Singh and Amit Panghal — finding themselves in the same weight-category draw.Sarita said her ward grabbed the opportunity with both hands."He then got a chance to compete in 55kg in the Nationals. Due to his effort, he won against the Services No.1, Olympians etc to be named Best Boxer in the Nationals. After that he got the chance to be part of the India camp," she said.He then cleared the final selection trials, which included physical assessments alongside ring performances."He participated in the final trial for the CWG and Asian Games — which had many aspects like strength and endurance tests before fighting in the ring. He won all of it to get selected for the CWG and was really happy and started training hard," she added.Just when Glasgow appeared certain, another setback emerged.Because Jadumani had only recently moved into 55kg, he did not possess the Asian ranking required under the Sports Ministry's eligibility criteria for Commonwealth Games selection."He got an explanation mail from the Sports Ministry, which put him in immense tension ahead of the Games," Sarita recalled.Under the ministry's guidelines, boxers were expected to be ranked among Asia's top eight in their respective categories."He was ranked No. 2 in 50kg, but he lacked a ranking in the new 55kg category. He had only competed in one Asian Championship in the new weight category before the trials for CWG and, being new to the category, lost in the quarterfinals," she said.That led to fresh doubts over his selection."He was disheartened when questions were raised whether he was a medal prospect because he was not in the rankings prescribed by the ministry. He called me and said the coaches were saying he may or may not be on the flight to the CWG because of this letter from the ministry," she recalled.The uncertainty only ended after BFI submitted a detailed explanation to the ministry, outlining Jadumani's circumstances following his weight-category switch."BFI replied to the ministry properly, explaining everything and after a lot of effort his ticket to Glasgow was approved. What I like about him is that he is the kind of person who doesn't give up and has a very strong will power," she said.Jadumani eventually reached the final after four demanding contests, each won by an identical 5-0 margin. But Sarita believes the scheduling ultimately worked against him."Jadumani's four bouts were very tough. He played all out in all the bouts till the semifinals as he got proper rest and recovery time. Since the gold medal opponent got a bye earlier, he had fewer bouts than Jadumani," she explained.The semifinal-final turnaround, she felt, proved decisive. There was a one-day gap after every bout until the semifinals, but there was no gap between the semifinal and final in Glasgow."Jadumani fought his semifinal in the evening and got the final bout the next morning only, so he did not get much time for recovery. If it was in the evening, he could have fought better. When he entered the ring for the final, I saw his face and body language sitting here and realised he had not had enough recovery," she said.The experience, she believes, underlines the growing importance of sports science."In such situations, we should look for how we can enhance or speed up the recovery process through sports science. We should discuss it to make sure our boxers can give 100 per cent every time they enter the ring," she added.Sarita first noticed Jadumani as a youngster competing in a local tournament."When I saw Jadumani for the first time, it was a tournament for young boys. His movement was really pleasing and I thought he could become a good boxer in the future. I identified him at that time only and gave him Rs 500 because I was very pleased with his performance," she recalled."Jadumani did not start with me from the grassroots. He learnt his basics from another academy. He came to my academy when he was preparing to enrol in the Army Sports Institute in Pune. At that time, I did not have any infrastructure and was coaching from a makeshift setup. And then Covid happened, we had to train in a very isolated small makeshift place,” she added.Years later, after training together through difficult Covid-19 conditions and watching him overcome one hurdle after another, Sarita believes Glasgow is only the beginning."We missed gold at the CWG, but we will work hard to get gold at the Asian Games for sure," she said.The bigger ambition, however, stretches far beyond continental success."His first and primary target remains Olympic gold. Commonwealth Games and Asian Games are the stepping stones in that journey. He will try to win India's first Olympic gold medal in boxing," Sarita concluded.
Article Summary: Jadumani Singh Mandengbam won silver at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. The 22-year-old Manipuri boxer won four consecutive unanimous 5-0 verdicts to storm into the bantamweight final before settling for silver against Australia's Jye Dixon. His medal also formed part of India's historic boxing campaign, which yielded seven golds and three silvers, making the country the No. 1 boxing nation at the Games.

Article Title: Days after historic CWG gold, Dilip Gavit leaves without meeting Raj Thackeray after two-hour wait
Article Text:
India's Dilip Mahadu Gavit (PTI Photo)

Invited, but left waiting

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A champion who made history in Glasgow

A journey built on resilience

Just days after scripting history for Indian para athletics at the Commonwealth Games, gold medallist Dilip Gavit found himself making headlines for a very different reason. The 23-year-old sprinter, who became India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the men's 100m T47 event, waited for nearly two hours to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray in Nashik on Thursday before leaving without the meeting taking place.According to Gavit's coach quoted by PTI, Vaijanath Kale, the para-athlete had been invited to meet Thackeray during the MNS chief's visit to Nashik. However, despite arriving at the scheduled venue, Gavit and his coach were made to wait for nearly two hours. A video from the venue showed MNS workers requesting the duo to wait longer while trying to explain that Thackeray was occupied."We were waiting for quite some time... Sir is busy. We will meet him later," Kale is heard saying in the video before they eventually left.The incident came just days after Gavit delivered one of India's biggest moments at the Commonwealth Games. Clocking a Games-record 10.71 seconds, the Nashik sprinter won the men's 100m T47 gold medal, leading a historic Indian one-two finish alongside Mohammed Basil Morssinganakath, who claimed silver. The victory marked India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medal in para athletics 100m T47.Gavit's success carries a deeper significance given his remarkable journey. Born into an economically disadvantaged tribal family in Maharashtra, he lost his right arm in a childhood accident. His life changed when coach Vaijanath Kale took him under his wing at the age of 12, supporting his education and athletic development. After winning gold in Glasgow, Gavit emotionally dedicated the medal to Kale, crediting his coach for transforming his life.
Article Summary: Dilip Gavit was invited to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray. The 23-year-old sprinter waited for nearly two hours for the meeting to take place. The incident came just days after he became India's first Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the men's 100m T47 event.

Article Title: How Harsh fought through pain to script CWG history, now targets Asiad medal
Article Text:
How judoka Harsh overcame pain

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Harsh Singh's right knee still swells. It still hurts. Every time the Indian judoka steps onto the mat, he is reminded of the ACL and meniscus tear that nearly derailed his career. But at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, pain took a back seat as the 23-year-old scripted history by becoming India's first-ever men's judo gold medallist."The pain never really goes away," Singh told TOI in an interview on Thursday. "Sometimes my knee still swells up and feels tight. During the CWG, I felt the pain and the knee occasionally got swollen. After surgery, the joint never became exactly the way it was before. There's always a little discomfort during fights. You have to ignore it and continue. The medal kept me going."The historic triumph came less than a year after Singh tore his ACL and meniscus while training at the Inspire Institute of Sport (IIS) in Aug 2025. Surgery followed in Oct last in Bengaluru before a year-long rehabilitation helped him return to competition."I was in rehabilitation for almost a year. The entire coaching team at the IIS, recovery specialists and Spencer sir (Mackay, S&C expert) helped me throughout.They rebuilt my strength step by step. Because of the IIS and their entire team, I was able to come back on the mat, qualify for the CWG and represent India," he said.The comeback demanded another battle off the mat. Months away from competition saw his weight rise to nearly 72kg, forcing him to shed more than 12kg to return to his 60kg category. Gold at a ranking tournament and bronze at the senior National championships sealed his place in India's CWG squad.Despite lingering discomfort, Singh dominated in Glasgow, with only a hard-fought semifinal stretching him before he clinched the historic title."The semifinal (against the Australian Pedro Carlos) was the toughest. In the 60kg category, even a small point can decide the match. We didn't want to concede anything and stayed aggressive," he recalled.With CWG gold secured, Singh has already shifted his attention to next year's Asian Games. Training stints in Japan and South Korea are part of his preparations as he looks to bridge the gap with Asia's best."I want to improve my speed, grip and strength. Japanese and Korean players are very fast, so training there will help," he said.Born into a modest family, with his father working as a daily-wage labourer, Singh once trained without owning a judo uniform. Support from the govt's schemes and a privately funded athletes' training centre changed the course of his career."My life has changed because of this medal. More people have started noticing judo," he said. "But the best compliment came from my family. They told me, 'You have made the entire family proud.' That meant more than anything else."Having conquered injury to create CWG history, Singh's next aim is clear — turning a gritty comeback into an Asian Games podium finish.
Article Summary: Harsh Singh became India's first-ever men's judo gold medallist. The 23-year-old tore his ACL and meniscus while training at the Inspire Institute of Sport. Surgery followed in Oct last in Bengaluru before a year-long rehabilitation helped him return to competition.

Article Title: Reality check after Commonwealth Games 2026: India’s boxing renaissance to face ultimate Asian exam
Article Text:
New Delhi, Aug 04 (ANI): Union Minister Kiren Rijiju in a group photograph with Indian boxing contingent (@KirenRijiju X/ANI Photo)
